exceptions.justification: A Windows 95 stub (returns 0), asked for by libmsvcrt's _vscprintf.o, _scprintf.o and wassert.o. The disassembly of _init_vscprintf shows the failure is anticipated: a null GetModuleHandleW makes mingw branch to its own _emu_vscprintf implementation, built on strlen/malloc/vsnprintf. The stub therefore selects the portable fallback, which is the intended behaviour here. Nothing is lost.

A Windows 95 stub (returns 0), asked for by libwinpthread's thread.o and sched.o, which the posix threading model and libstdc++'s static linking bring into every C++ binary - including through <chrono> alone. It is only reached through pthread_join and pthread_cancel, where it is far from harmless: pthread_join tests its return and takes its error path, so std::thread::join() throws under Windows 95. That is one of the reasons the E02-S01 layer exists, whose dkr_thread_join goes through WaitForSingleObject. What makes the import harmless is structural and not hoped for: check-cpp-subset.py forbids <thread> on the target, so no project code can reach pthread_join. The two guard rails compose. WITNESS.EXE is the exception within the exception - it is E00-S02's witness, whose role is precisely to exercise std::thread, and where the symbol is genuinely reachable.

A Windows 95 stub (returns 0), asked for by libmsvcrt's rand_s.o, itself pulled in by libstdc++'s std::random_device::_M_getentropy - which the mere presence of std::filesystem::path in a binary brings in. rand_s calls LoadLibraryW then GetProcAddress to reach the system generator; under Windows 95 it therefore obtains a null function pointer. What is tolerated here is the *presence* of the import, which does not stop the load. What is not, and must be remembered: **std::random_device does not work on this target**, and calling it would jump through a null pointer. No project code uses it; verified that manipulating std::filesystem::path does not touch it - the FSPATH.EXE probe returns correct results on the machine.

A Windows 95 stub (returns 0), asked for by libwinpthread_la-clock.o, which <chrono> brings in wholesale - the file carries clock_gettime and clock_getres together. The disassembly of clock.o says which serves what: clock_gettime calls QueryPerformanceCounter for CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and GetProcessTimes or GetThreadTimes only for the process-time clock ids; clock_getres calls GetSystemTimeAdjustment for CLOCK_REALTIME. std::chrono::steady_clock, the only clock this code uses, takes the QueryPerformanceCounter branch - the one E02-S03 measured on the machine. The process-time clock ids are asked for neither by libstdc++ nor by the project. The tolerance covers the test binaries, which use <chrono>; it does not extend to the game.

Exported with real code, and it refuses all the same: E02-S05 measured it on the machine, MoveFileExA(REPLACE_EXISTING) returns ERROR_CALL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. It is the third category of unavailable API, the one no static analysis sees. It is asked for by libstdc++'s fs_ops.o, that is, by std::filesystem::rename - which this code does not call on this target, E02-S05's indirection point going through dkr_file_rename and its delete-then-rename sequence. The import is therefore present and unreachable. The game is now linked, and the re-examination has taken place: save_manager called MoveFileExW directly under #if defined(_WIN32), which E02-S06 fixed by routing it through the indirection point. The import that remains comes from libstdc++'s fs_ops.o, reached only through std::filesystem::rename, which no project code calls any more on this target.

A Windows 95 stub (returns 0). Asked for by librecomp's mods.cpp to load a native mod - a compiled DLL. The function itself only exists from Windows NT4/98 in this form, and its LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_* flags date from Windows 7. The stub therefore returns a null handle, and loading the mod fails cleanly through the error path already provided. That is the intended behaviour: native mods cannot work on this target, and the mod system has been out of scope since E00-S01. What matters is that the failure is an operation's, not the program's load.

A Windows 95 stub (returns 0). Asked for by N64Recomp's analysis.cpp, cgenerator.cpp and recompilation.cpp - not by their code, but by fmt, the formatting header they use, which writes to the console through the wide API when it detects a terminal. The stub makes that write fail, and fmt does not test it: the on-the-fly recompiler's diagnostic messages will not appear on this machine. It is a degradation, and it is accepted as such - those messages concern only mod recompilation, already out of scope. Nothing the player sees goes through there.
